Tuesday. Kavitha asked, for the third time, if she could cook dinner. Pradeep's mother waved her off and reached for the pressure cooker. Kavitha bit back a sharp reply and stood in the doorway, annoyed and a little shut out.

Friday. From the balcony she watched Amma move the spice tins around for the second time that week. Kavitha said quietly to nobody, "She isn't saying my cooking is bad. She's saying she doesn't want to be someone the house can run without." The thought sat oddly warm in her chest.

Sunday. "Amma, will you teach me your rasam? I'll chop and you decide the tadka." Amma's hands paused, then she pulled a second stool to the counter. It was not smooth; they argued over the tamarind. But Amma was humming when Pradeep came in.

qa.q: What did Kavitha ask Amma to teach her on Sunday?
qa.a: Kavitha asked Amma to teach her rasam, offering to chop while Amma decided the tadka.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling on Tuesday when she was waved away from the cooker?
qa.a: Kavitha felt annoyed and a little shut out; she bit back a sharp reply and stood in the doorway.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha try if Amma still wanted to run the whole kitchen?
qa.a: Kavitha could ask Amma to plan the week's menu while Kavitha cooks some of it, because that answers the wish to be needed instead of only pushing back.

qa.q: How might Sunday have felt to Amma?
qa.a: Amma may have felt valued, since she was asked for her skill and given the tadka to decide, which fits the humming.

grounding: Kavitha reads Amma's insistence on cooking as a wish to be needed and finds a way to include her.

Joseph, you're struggling with your wife and your mother in the kitchen? Let me, Vinita, your grandmother, tell you what I learned as a new bride in Kottayam.
My mother-in-law cooked everything. Every meal, every day. If I tried to make even the fish curry, she would take the spoon from my hand. At first I thought she didn't trust me.
Then one evening I saw her sitting alone after dinner, when everyone had praised the fish. Her face was so happy. And I understood: it wasn't about me. After her husband died, the kitchen was where she still mattered.
So I stopped trying to take it over. I asked her to teach me her fish curry. Then I asked her to plan the Sunday lunches, while I did the weekday cooking.
She became my best friend in that house, Joseph. Look for what the demand is protecting.

qa.q: Where was Vinita a new bride?
What did Vinita realise about her mother-in-law's feelings after seeing her sit alone after dinner?
qa.a: Vinita realised the mother-in-law felt happy and valued when cooking; after being widowed, the kitchen was where she still felt needed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vinita's story, and what choice followed?
qa.a: The turning point was seeing the mother-in-law's happy face after dinner; Vinita chose to ask to learn her recipes and let her plan Sunday lunches instead of resisting.

qa.q: How might the mother-in-law have felt when asked to teach the fish curry?
qa.a: She likely felt respected and needed, which is why she later became like a best friend.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how a wife saw that her mother-in-law's insistence on cooking came from wanting to feel needed and found ways to include her.

Deepika had a client presentation at four, the flat's kitchen was the size of a cupboard, and her mother-in-law was there again, insisting on making lunch for everyone.
"Mummyji, I've already planned dal and rice," Deepika said, trying not to snap.
"Your dal has no taste. Let me do it."
Deepika went back to her laptop, jaw tight. Then she remembered what Vishal had said last week: since his father retired and his sister moved to Canada, his mother hardly had anyone to look after.
She looked at the kitchen again. Mummyji was humming.
Maybe this wasn't about the dal. Maybe it was about being needed.
At lunch, Deepika said, "Mummyji, would you take over Sunday lunches? Your rajma is better than anything I make. And on weekdays I'll cook, since I'm home anyway."
Her mother-in-law's face softened. "Only Sundays?"
"Only Sundays. And teach me the rajma."

qa.q: What time was Deepika's client presentation?
What did Deepika think was behind her mother-in-law's insistence on cooking?
qa.a: Deepika thought Mummyji felt lonely and wanted to feel needed, since Vishal's father had retired and his sister had moved away.

qa.q: What else could Deepika try if Sunday lunches weren't enough?
qa.a: She could invite her mother-in-law to plan meals for festivals or teach a dish each month, giving her a clear, valued role.

qa.q: How might Mummyji see Deepika's offer?
qa.a: Mummyji likely feels appreciated and included, with a role of her own rather than being pushed out of the kitchen.

grounding: It shows a wife noticing that her mother-in-law's insistence on cooking comes from wanting to feel needed and finding a way to include her.
